beats.text: 2022: the team is built around him

script: Watch Messi at the 2026 World Cup. Most of the match, he's walking. Pedro El Ingeniero broke it down: sixty-four percent of his distance was at walking pace. The average forward walked half as much. Yet in his first four World Cups, young and explosive, Messi scored six goals. In the last two, at thirty-five and thirty-nine, he scored fifteen. How? Go back to 2007. Right winger, fifty meters from goal. He runs, beats his man, shoots. 2009. Guardiola makes him a false nine. 2014. He stops reaching the box and starts deciding who does. 2017. He stays up top and stops tracking back. 2022. Scaloni builds the whole team around him. Five coaches. Five positions. Every time they took something away, he won more. At the 2026 World Cup, Harry Kane made about six hundred high-speed runs. Messi made two hundred ninety-eight, and still scored eight. Because when he walks, he scans. By the time the ball arrives, he already knows what to do. Less running. More thinking.
caption:
Messi walks more than almost anyone on the field. And he scores more. 🐐

64% of his distance at the 2026 World Cup was at walking pace, and the average forward walked about half as much.
First four World Cups, running everywhere: 6 goals.
Last two, at 35 and 39: 15 goals.
Harry Kane made about 600 high-speed runs at the 2026 World Cup. Messi made 298, and still scored 8.

How he got there: winger at 20, false nine under Guardiola, the playmaker who decides who scores, then the player a whole national team is built around. Five coaches, five positions, and every time they took something away, he won more.

The trick: while he walks, he scans. By the time the ball comes, he already knows what to do with it.

Who's the Messi on your team, walking all game and still scoring? Tag them 👇

Numbers and 3D analysis: Pedro El Ingeniero, from his video "¿Por qué Messi dejó de correr a los 24?" on YouTube (@PedroElIngeniero). Watch the full breakdown there, it's worth it.
